extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century literate public interested in manners, theatre, and morals
extracted.subtask_description: Short, satirical/moral essays for a periodical (The Spectator) addressing social manners, theatre, and public taste using anecdotes and commentary. These pieces both criticize entertainments and offer prescriptions for behaviour and artistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve character in masquerade
rubrics_metrics.description: Maskers should 'preserve their Characters' in assemblies and behave in ways fitting their dress/role rather than dressing as one thing and acting as another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: read the source romances or models (e.g., 'the Arcadia') before appearing; avoid mismatches (examples given: 'Rakes in the Habit of Roman Senators, and grave Politicians in the Dress of Rakes'; a Nymph with a Crook speaking in 'the pert Stile of the Pit Bawdry'; a Philosopher made speechless). The organiser should admonish the town and encourage maskers to 'say or do things proper for the Dress in which he appears.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors should use expressive physical action and significant looks
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedians ought to employ arms, legs, and expressive faces to convey passion — imitation of the best (e.g., Nicolini) would improve English tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance drawn from praise of Nicolini: 'Could they make the same use of their Arms and Legs, and inform their Faces with as significant Looks and Passions, how glorious would an English Tragedy appear...' Use of physical action gives dignity to language that might otherwise seem forced or unnatural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on printed promises — manage audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers should be careful about printed bills that raise expectations which the stage cannot fulfil (e.g., promised chariots or grand thunder and lightning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: printed opera disappointed when promised Chariot/white horses did not appear; advice implied: either avoid overpromising or ensure stagecraft meets advertised spectacle. Contrast noted: Powell forbear'd to give a bill beforehand so 'every Scene is new and unexpected.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage machinery and scenery must be coherent and competently managed
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery and stage mechanisms should be uniform, changed appropriately, and timed with dexterity to maintain illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: criticism where side-scenes weren't changed and the audience was presented 'with a Prospect of the Ocean in the midst of a delightful Grove.' Positive note: the boy directing painted dragons 'flash'd out his Rosin in such just Proportions, and in such due Time.' Also specific operator tips: 'keeping his Head a little lower, and hiding his Candle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Animals introduced on stage must be disciplined and trained
rubrics_metrics.description: If animals are used in performance they should be trained to perform their parts rather than disrupt the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-examples: sparrows and chaffinches flew irregularly, perching in galleries or putting out candles; positive example: Powell's pig was disciplined and danced a Minuet with Punch. Implicit standard: animals should contribute to, not degrade, the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performances should favour intelligibility and native language where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Language and vocal delivery matter; performances in the audience's language and with appropriate vocal quality enhance comprehension and enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: some opera heroes' 'squeak of their Voices' makes them seem 'Eunuchs'; the author prefers Powell's English performance because 'it is in our own Language.' Implicit recommendation: match language and vocal style to audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience taste should be governed by common sense rather than mere show
rubrics_metrics.description: Public entertainment should avoid degrading into childish or merely showy diversions; true taste requires good sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: 'our present Grievance does not seem to be the Want of a good Taste, but of Common Sense.' Implicit counsel to both audiences and producers: favour substance over superficial pomp; avoid amusements that are 'only grown more childish, not more innocent.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect children from fostering irrational terrors
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents should guard children against stories and entertainments that cultivate fear and imaginary horrors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale and examples: Narratives of ghosts and apparitions can 'craz[e]' imaginations and leave lasting fear (a boy too frightened to go to bed alone). Remedy: 'arm our selves against them by the Dictates of Reason and Religion' and 'preserve my Children from these little Horrours of Imagination.'
